@graph.headline: Why Do Most Traders Lose Money in India? The Real Reasons (and the Exact Fixes)

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the 90% figure describes individual traders in the equity F&O segment, where leverage, short-dated options, and high frequency combine. SEBI's studies found roughly 90-91% of individual F&O traders incurred net losses in each year from FY22 to FY25, easing to 87.7% in FY26. The main drivers are oversized positions, overtrading, options time decay, and transaction costs — not a lack of entry signals. The fix is 1% risk per trade, a daily loss limit, capped trade frequency, and counted costs.

mainEntity.name: Why do 90% of traders lose money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beginners lose mainly because they trade before they have rules. They size positions by gut feel instead of stop-loss math, trade without a daily loss limit, copy tips without an exit plan, and buy short-dated options without understanding time decay. They also expect income too early, which forces trades in conditions where they have no edge. The remedy is to write the rules down, risk 1% per trade, cap trades at 3 per day, and judge the first 50 trades on rule-following rather than profit.

mainEntity.name: Why do beginners lose money in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for most retail traders, for specific mechanical reasons. Options involve leverage, time decay, and expiry: a bought option loses value every day even if the underlying does not move, and it can expire worthless, losing the entire premium. Plain cash delivery stock purchases, bought with your own money, cannot lose more than the amount invested and have no expiry clock. SEBI's FY26 data reflects this: options accounted for about 92% of individual F&O losses.

mainEntity.name: Is options trading riskier than stocks?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the product. In a plain cash delivery trade bought with your own money, no — the maximum loss is the amount invested. In leveraged positions such as futures, options selling, or margin-funded trades, yes — losses can exceed the margin posted, because you control a much larger exposure than your deposit. The broker can issue a margin call demanding more funds, or square off the position, possibly locking in a loss larger than the original deposit.

mainEntity.name: Can you lose more money than you invest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, through two channels. First, every trade adds transaction costs — STT, exchange charges, and brokerage — so frequency directly increases the cost drag on the account. Second, trade quality falls as frequency rises: the first few trades of the day are usually the planned ones, while later trades are typically driven by boredom, FOMO, or revenge after a loss. Capping trades at 3 planned setups per day is the practical fix.

Control losses with rules decided before trading, not with willpower during trading. Risk no more than 1% of your account per trade, computed from your stop-loss distance. Set a daily loss limit of 2-3% and stop for the day when it hits, ideally enforced by your broker's kill-switch feature. Place every stop-loss as a live order, never as a mental note. Cap trades at 3 per day. Avoid averaging down on losing trades unless the written plan allowed it in advance.

mainEntity.name: How can traders control their losses?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be, but the data says it is difficult. SEBI's equity cash-segment study found 7 out of 10 individual intraday traders made losses in FY2023. Intraday trading compresses every common cause of losses into a few hours: more trades, more costs, faster emotional decisions, and no overnight recovery time. It becomes viable only with the full discipline stack — 1% risk per trade, a daily loss limit, capped frequency, counted costs, and a written plan followed for at least 50 trades before judging results.
